title: The ecology of schools
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau draws on ecologist Eugene Odum's framework to argue that schools should be understood as ecosystems rather than machines — complex adaptive systems defined by feedback loops, relationships, and emergent properties that cannot be engineered into existence by management intervention. He challenges the school improvement paradigm that treats educational outcomes as mechanical outputs of discrete interventions, showing instead that outcomes emerge from the quality of relationships and information flows throughout the whole system. Didau introduces concepts of ecological succession, resilience, and energy flow as lenses for understanding why some schools recover from disruption while others collapse. He argues that applying interventions to complex systems without ecological understanding tends to produce unexpected consequences or failure, and that the most important things about school quality — trust, morale, collective belief — are precisely the least measurable. The article concludes that improving schools requires attending to their ecology before reaching for the next intervention programme.
points: Schools are ecosystems, not machines — their outcomes are emergent properties of relationships and feedback loops, not outputs of discrete manageable interventions.
Eugene Odum's ecological framework reveals that school improvement efforts often fail because they target individual parts while ignoring the dynamics of the whole system.
Resilient schools, like resilient ecosystems, maintain their function through disruption because of the quality of internal relationships, not organisational structures.
The most important things about school quality — trust, morale, collective identity and belief — are precisely what accountability and management frameworks most consistently overlook.
Applying interventions to a complex adaptive system without understanding its ecological dynamics produces unpredictable and often counterproductive results.
quotes: There’s the site manager whose knowledge meant he could spot problems long before anyone else noticed them; the head’s PA who knew everyone and kept relationships running smoothly; the wise old teaching assistant who understood the most vulnerable children inside out and would know exactly what to do no matter what went wrong.

Building on Malthus’s observation that populations are constrained by finite resources, Pierre François Verhulst developed the logistic model of population growth, showing that populations cannot increase indefinitely but eventually level off as they approach the limits of their environment.

When it works, the result is a healthier organisational ecology, in which ideas spread more quickly, innovation becomes less dependent on chance encounters and valuable knowledge is less likely to disappear when experienced colleagues move on.

Cross-department planning, coaching, subject associations, mentoring, instructional coaching and protected time for professional conversation can all increase the number and quality of connections through which knowledge can travel.

Instead of viewing schools as collections of discrete parts assembled into a functioning whole, we might understand them as living systems: dynamic networks of relationships, feedback loops, dependencies and adaptation.

Thinking of schools as machines and people as components to optimise may produce short term gains, but it also risks creating organisations that are efficient without being healthy, productive without being resilient.

In many ways, the turn towards the science of learning has served us well, displacing a good deal of wishful thinking and making the profession more sceptical of confident assertions unsupported by robust research..
